summary: Fast compilation, cheap goroutine concurrency, explicit error handling, and single static binaries powering cloud infrastructure.

rows.means: declares the executable package name and imports standard libraries
rows.consequence: Go compilers reject unused imports with a build error, guaranteeing clean dependency trees.

rows.means: defines a function with multiple return values
rows.consequence: Returning the result and an error together is the foundation of Go's explicit error handling pattern.

rows.means: declares and initializes a variable with inferred type
rows.consequence: Only valid inside function bodies. For package-level globals, use var Name string = "val".

rows.means: composite data type with field definitions and reflection tags
rows.consequence: Struct tags provide metadata for serialization (JSON, XML, DB). Fields starting with a capital letter are public/exported.

rows.code: type Reader interface { Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) }
rows.means: implicit interface satisfied automatically by any matching type
rows.consequence: Types do not declare 'implements Reader'. If a type provides the method signature, it satisfies the interface automatically.

rows.means: allocates and initializes slices, maps, or channels in memory
rows.consequence: Required for reference types; unlike new(), which only zeroes memory, make sets up internal pointer buffers.

rows.means: appends items to a slice, growing capacity when full
rows.consequence: If capacity is exceeded, append allocates a new larger backing array and copies elements over, returning a new slice header.

rows.means: iterates over slices, arrays, maps, and channels
rows.consequence: Go has only one looping keyword: for. It handles traditional loops, while-loops, and range iterations.

rows.means: schedules a function call to run when the surrounding function returns
rows.consequence: Arguments are evaluated immediately, but execution is deferred until function exit. Ideal for f.Close() or mu.Unlock().

rows.means: launches a function on a lightweight concurrent goroutine
rows.consequence: Goroutines begin with only a ~2KB memory stack that grows and shrinks dynamically, allowing millions of concurrent tasks.

rows.code: chan Type and ch <- val / val := <-ch
rows.means: typed channel pipe: send value / receive value
rows.consequence: "Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating." Enables safe synchronization between goroutines.
Blocks until one of its cases can proceed. If multiple cases are ready, one is chosen via pseudo-random selection.

rows.code: if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed: %w", err) }
rows.consequence: No hidden exceptions. Errors are normal values that must be inspected and propagated upward explicitly.

rows.means: synchronization counter waiting for a collection of goroutines to finish
rows.consequence: wg.Add(1) increments the counter; wg.Done() decrements it; wg.Wait() blocks execution until the counter reaches zero.

rows.means: mutual exclusion lock guarding critical shared memory regions
rows.consequence: Always follow mu.Lock() immediately with defer mu.Unlock() to prevent deadlocks when functions exit early on errors.

rows.means: carries deadlines, cancellation signals, and request-scoped values
rows.consequence: Enables propagating cancellation across network calls and child goroutines when an HTTP client disconnects.

rows.means: triggers catastrophic unwind / recovers control inside deferred function
rows.consequence: Reserved exclusively for truly unrecoverable conditions (e.g. nil pointer dereference, out-of-bounds memory).

rows.means: type assertion checking dynamic interface value
rows.consequence: If ok is true, val contains the concrete type. If ok is false, prevents a panic and allows safe fallback.
